title: My life story
cando: tell the story of your life, and talk about past habits and turning points

about.text: In this lesson you tell the story of your life: where you grew up, what you used to do, and the turning points that changed your life. You read how one town changed after its factory closed down, and you tell your own story for a community history project.
goals: Tell your life story in order, from your childhood to now.
Talk about past habits with used to and would: I used to live by the sea.
Use grow up, bring up and settle down correctly.
Read an article and a form about a town's past, and write about then and now.
Describe a turning point, and say what you decided.

chapters.title: A turning point
chapters.text:
Everyone has a life story, and most life stories have a turning point: a moment when your life went in a new direction.
In this lesson, you tell your own story. But first, you listen to Kwame. He's a bus driver, and he's going to retire at the end of the week. At lunch, his colleague Priya asks him about his life.
Listen for three useful phrases. When I was younger… I grew up in… That's when I decided to…
When Kwame was young, he had a big ambition. Listen for what it was, what happened to it, and who helped him at the time.

chapters.title: used to and would
chapters.text:
Now, the grammar. When we talk about the past, we often use used to. I used to live by the sea. I used to be very shy. It means: this was true for a long time, but it isn't true now.
We can also use would, for things we did again and again. Every Saturday, my grandfather would take me to the match.
But be careful. Would is only for actions. For states, like be, have, live and like, use used to. So: I used to have long hair. Not: I would have long hair.
In questions and negatives, the d disappears. Did you use to work here? I didn't use to like coffee.
You also learn three verbs for a life story. You grow up in a place. Someone brings you up. And later, you settle down.

chapters.title: Then and now
chapters.text:
Next, you read an article by Ruth. She grew up in a small town where one factory employed almost everyone. When she was fourteen, the factory closed down.
Read it once for the main idea: how did the town change? Then read the form she filled in for a community history project.
Look for the words that show then and now: in those days, nowadays, compared with.
After that, you write two paragraphs about a place you know. First, what it used to be like. Then, what it's like nowadays.

chapters.title: Your story in two minutes
chapters.text:
Then you tell your life story for a community history project. You only have two minutes, so plan it first.
Tell it in four parts, in order. Where you grew up. What you used to do. Your turning point. And your life now.
Don't write every sentence on paper. Write a few key words, and speak.
At the end, say how you feel when you look back. For example: Looking back, I'm glad I left home. Or: Looking back, I'm glad I changed my mind.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story about someone's life. Read it once for the story, and look for the turning point. Then read it again and answer the questions.
Finally, compare the story with your own life. Was your turning point bigger or smaller?

warmup.prompt: Think about your life so far. What was your biggest turning point?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Everyone's life is different, and many people have more than one turning point. In this lesson, you talk about yours.

conversation.title: Kwame's last week
conversation.setting: Kwame is retiring on Friday after thirty years as a bus driver. At lunch, his younger colleague Priya asks him about his life.
lines: Priya
So, Kwame, only four more days. Are you ready to retire?
Kwame
I think so. It feels strange, though. I've driven buses here for thirty years.
Priya
Did you always want to be a driver?
Kwame
Not at all. When I was younger, my big ambition was to play football.
Priya
Really? Where did you grow up?
Kwame
I grew up in a small town by the sea. My grandparents brought me up.
Priya
What was your childhood like?
Kwame
Very happy. Every Saturday, my grandfather would take me to watch the local team, and I used to practise on the beach every evening.
Priya
So what happened?
Kwame
When I was eighteen, I hurt my knee badly. At the time, I thought my life was over.
Priya
Oh no. What did you do?
Kwame
My uncle drove buses in the city, and he encouraged me to try it. That's when I decided to leave home.
Priya
So that was the turning point.
Kwame
Exactly. I moved to the city, got married and settled down. Looking back, I wouldn't change a thing.

questions.why: Kwame says: My grandparents brought me up.

questions.q: What did Kwame use to do every evening?
questions.why: He says: I used to practise on the beach every evening.

questions.a: to try driving buses in the city
wrong: to play for a football team
questions.why: His uncle encouraged him to try driving buses, and that's when he decided to leave home.

phrases.text: When I was younger, my big ambition was to play football.
phrases.use: Starting to talk about your past.

phrases.text: I grew up in a small town by the sea.
phrases.use: Saying where you lived as a child.
Saying who looked after you as a child.
Asking someone about their early life.

phrases.text: At the time, I thought my life was over.
phrases.use: Saying how you felt then, not now.

phrases.text: That's when I decided to leave home.
phrases.use: Saying what you chose at an important moment.

phrases.text: Looking back, I wouldn't change a thing.
phrases.use: Saying how you feel about your past now.

items.meaning: The early part of your life, before you are a teenager.
items.example: I spent most of my childhood in a village near the coast.

items.meaning: Between the ages of thirteen and nineteen.
items.example: In my teenage years, I worked in my uncle's shop every summer.

items.meaning: One period in a longer process, or in your life.
items.example: At that stage of my life, I just wanted to earn some money.

items.meaning: A moment when your life, or a situation, starts to go in a new direction.
items.example: Losing that job was a turning point: I went back to college.

items.meaning: Something you really want to do or become in the future.
items.example: Her ambition is to open her own restaurant.

items.meaning: A chance to do something good or useful.
items.example: The job in Dubai was a great opportunity, so I took it.

items.meaning: A person or thing that changes the way you think or act.
items.example: My first manager was a big influence on me.

items.meaning: To give someone support, so they feel they can do something.
items.example: My wife encouraged me to apply for the job.

items.meaning: The feeling that you can do something well.
items.example: The course gave me the confidence to speak in meetings.

items.meaning: To think about something that happened in your past.
items.example: When I look back, I'm glad I took the risk.

items.meaning: To stop living with your parents and start living on your own.
items.example: I left home at nineteen and moved to the city.

items.meaning: To leave your home and go to live in a different one.
items.example: We moved house four times before we settled down.

items.meaning: To stop working, usually because you are older.
items.example: My father retired at sixty-five, and now he grows vegetables.

items.meaning: To make a new decision that is different from your first one.
items.example: I wanted to study law, but then I changed my mind.

items.meaning: Then, when it was happening, and not now.
items.example: At the time, I was angry. Now I understand why she did it.

sound.title: used to
sound.explain: In used to, the d is silent, and the s sounds like the s in juice, not the z in news. Say it like one short word: yoost-tuh. But the verb use, as in I use my phone every day, has a z sound. Listen, then say each group.
lines: I used to work nights.
We used to live by the sea.
I didn't use to like it.
I use my phone for everything.

sayIt.instructions: Say Kwame's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Is used to short and smooth?
lines: When I was younger, my big ambition was to play football.
I grew up in a small town by the sea. My grandparents brought me up.
Every Saturday, my grandfather would take me to watch the local team, and I used to practise on the beach every evening.
My uncle drove buses in the city, and he encouraged me to try it. That's when I decided to leave home.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. They all talk about Kwame's past, but in different ways.
examples: I used to practise on the beach every evening.
Every Saturday, my grandfather would take me to watch the local team.
When I was eighteen, I hurt my knee badly.
spot.question: Which two sentences are about things Kwame did again and again? Which one is about one event at one time? And what does brought me up mean?
spot.answer: used to + verb and would + verb are for past habits: things Kwame did again and again. I hurt my knee is the past simple: one event, at one time. Brought me up means his grandparents looked after him until he was an adult.

rules.title: used to and would for the past
rule: used to + verb: a habit or a state in the past that is not true now. I used to live by the sea.
would + verb: an action we did again and again in the past. Every Saturday, we would go to the match.
would is for actions only. For states like be, have, live and like, use used to: I used to have long hair.
Questions and negatives have no d: Did you use to work here? I didn't use to like it.
For one action at one time, use the past simple: I left home in 1998.
rules.mistake: used to is only for the past. Not: Nowadays I use to cycle to work. Say: Nowadays I usually cycle to work.

rules.title: grow up, bring up, settle down
rule: grow up = become an adult in a place: I grew up in Lagos.
bring someone up = look after a child until they are an adult: My aunt brought me up.
settle down = start a calm life in one place, often with a partner: We settled down in Leeds.
A pronoun goes in the middle: She brought us up. Not: She brought up us.
The past forms are grew up, brought up and settled down.
rules.mistake: Not: My grandmother grew me up. Say: My grandmother brought me up.

practice.q: When I was a child, we ___ play in the street until it got dark.
practice.why: would + verb for an action we did again and again in the past.

practice.q: I ___ be very shy, but now I love meeting people.
practice.why: be is a state, not an action, so we use used to, not would.

practice.q: Did you ___ work at the hospital?
practice.why: After did, we write use to, with no d.

practice.q: I ___ up in a small town in the north.
practice.why: grow up = become an adult in a place.

practice.q: My aunt ___ me up when my parents worked abroad.
practice.why: bring someone up = look after a child until they are an adult.

practice.q: They travelled for years, and then they settled ___ in Leeds.
practice.why: settle down = start a calm life in one place.

practice.q: In 2010 I ___ to Manchester for a new job.
practice.why: One action at one time: the past simple.
A pronoun like us goes in the middle: brought us up.

practice.q: I ___ like coffee, but now I drink three cups a day.
practice.why: like is a state, and the past negative is didn't use to.
used to is only for the past. For now, use the present simple: I usually cycle.

yourTurn.prompt: Think about your life ten or twenty years ago. Write four or five sentences: where you grew up, what you used to do, what you would do every week, and what is different now.
starters: When I was younger, I used to …
yourTurn.model: I grew up in a busy city near the coast. When I was younger, I used to work in my parents' shop after school. Every Saturday, I would help my father at the market. I didn't use to enjoy it, but I learned a lot about people. Nowadays I work in an office, and sometimes I miss the market.

text.title: The year the factory closed, and a community history form
text.body:
THE YEAR THE FACTORY CLOSED
by Ruth Ferreira
I grew up in Kettleford, a small town in the north of England with a population of about four thousand. For most of my childhood, the shoe factory at the end of our road employed nearly everyone. My mother worked there, and so did most of our neighbours.
In those days, the factory was the centre of our lives. People used to walk to work together at seven o'clock, and on Friday evenings the whole street would meet at the social club.
Then, in 1986, the factory closed down. I was fourteen. Suddenly, half the town was unemployed. My mother found work cleaning offices, and she would leave the house at five every morning.
Over the next decade, most of my generation moved away to find work. I stayed and trained as an electrician, which is what my mother had always wanted for me.
Nowadays Kettleford is a quiet place. Compared with the old days, there are more cafés and fewer jobs. Personally, I don't miss the factory, but I do miss those Friday evenings.

- - - - - - - -

PRACTICE FORM: this project does not exist.
KETTLEFORD COMMUNITY HISTORY PROJECT
We are recording the stories of people who have lived in the town for a long time.
Name: Ruth Ferreira
In Kettleford: from 1972 to now
Which years would you like to talk about? The 1980s
Was there a turning point? Yes: the shoe factory closed in 1986.
What changed for you personally? My mother had to find new work, and I decided to stay and train.
Who else should we talk to? My neighbour, whose father was the factory manager.
Interviews last about 40 minutes and are recorded. You can stop at any time.

gist.q: What is the article mainly about?
gist.a: how a town changed after its factory closed
wrong: how to find work in a shoe factory
why the writer moved to a big city
gist.why: Ruth describes Kettleford before and after the shoe factory closed down.

gist.a: offering to tell your story to a history project
wrong: applying for a job at the factory
gist.why: The project is recording the stories of people who have lived in the town for a long time.

detail.q: How old was Ruth when the factory closed down?
detail.why: She writes: Then, in 1986, the factory closed down. I was fourteen.

detail.q: What did most of Ruth's generation do?
detail.a: They moved away to find work.
wrong: They stayed and trained as electricians.
detail.why: Over the next decade, most of my generation moved away to find work.

detail.q: What does Ruth miss about the old days?
detail.a: the Friday evenings at the social club
wrong: the shops on the high street
detail.why: Personally, I don't miss the factory, but I do miss those Friday evenings.

detail.q: How long does an interview for the project last?
detail.why: The form says: Interviews last about 40 minutes and are recorded.

words.title: The town I grew up in

items.meaning: All the people who were born at about the same time.
items.example: My parents' generation often stayed in one job all their lives.

items.meaning: To pay someone to work for you.
items.example: The hospital employs over two thousand people.

items.meaning: Without a paid job, but wanting one.
items.example: He was unemployed for six months after the shop closed.

items.meaning: The number of people who live in a place.
items.example: The population of the town has grown to fifty thousand.

items.meaning: To stop doing business for ever. A shop, an office or a factory can do this.
items.example: The old cinema closed down when I was a teenager.

items.meaning: To leave your town or area and go to live somewhere else.
items.example: Most of my school friends moved away to find work.

items.meaning: A period of ten years.
items.example: The town changed more in one decade than in the fifty years before.

items.meaning: Used when you give your own opinion, or talk about yourself.
items.example: Personally, I think the town is better now.

items.meaning: In the past, at the time you are talking about.
items.example: In those days, nobody had a mobile phone.

items.meaning: At the present time, compared with the past.
items.example: Nowadays most people in the town work in shops or offices.

items.meaning: Used when you look at how two things are different.
items.example: Compared with London, rents here are very low.

model.title: Then and now: my home town
model.body:
I grew up in a small town in the east of Uganda. In those days, most people worked on farms, and my father used to cycle to his fields every morning. On Sundays, the whole family would walk to the market together. There was no internet, and very few people had a car.
Nowadays the town is much bigger, and many young people have moved away to the capital to find work. Compared with the old days, life is faster and more comfortable, but people have less time for each other. Personally, I miss the Sunday walks, but I don't miss the dusty roads!

write.task: Write about a place you know well, then and now. It can be your home town, your street or your workplace. Write two paragraphs of 80–120 words: what it used to be like, and what it is like nowadays.
write.starter: I grew up in … In those days, …
checklist: I used used to or would for things that happened again and again.
I used in those days and nowadays to show then and now.
I compared the two times, for example with compared with.
I wrote two paragraphs: one about then, and one about now.

card.title: Your story for the history project
card.situation: Your local library is recording people's life stories for a community history project. A volunteer, Lena, is interviewing you today. You have about two minutes to tell your story.
card.goal: Tell your life story in order: where you grew up, what you used to do, one turning point and your life now. Then answer Lena's question.

phrases: I grew up in … . My … brought me up.
When I was younger, I used to … .
The turning point came when … . That's when I decided to … .
prepare.notes: Make notes in four parts, in order: your childhood, your teenage years or your first job, one turning point, and your life now. Write key words only, not full sentences, so that you speak naturally.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is Lena from the history project. Tell your life story in two minutes while the others listen for your turning point. Then each listener asks you one question.
doIt.wehel: You are Lena, a volunteer for a community history project. You record people's life stories. Interview me. Ask me to tell my life story in about two minutes. Then ask me two questions, for example about my turning point or what I used to do. At the end, tell me one thing I did well and one thing I can do better. Use clear, simple English.

model.title: Carlos tells his story
lines: Lena
Thank you for coming in, Carlos. Could you start by telling me where you grew up?
You
Of course. I grew up in a village near Valencia, in Spain. My mother brought me up on her own.
Lena
What was life like in the village?
You
Very quiet. In the summer I used to help my uncle on his farm, and every evening the whole village would sit outside and talk.
Lena
And when did you come here?
You
In 1998. A friend offered me a job in a restaurant. At the time, I didn't speak any English at all.
Lena
That sounds difficult.
You
It was. But the owner encouraged me to go to evening classes. That was the turning point. My confidence grew, and five years later I became the manager.
Lena
And what about your life now?
You
Nowadays I run a small café on Market Street. I got married and settled down here, and my two children have grown up.
Lena
Looking back, would you change anything?
You
Not really. Well, maybe I'd start learning English earlier!
Lena
Thank you, Carlos. That's a wonderful story.
compare: Did you tell your story in order: your childhood, a turning point, your life now?
Did you use used to or would for past habits?
Did you say what the turning point was, and what you decided?
Did you say how you feel when you look back?

I can talk about past habits with used to and would.
I can use grow up, bring up and settle down correctly.

reading.before: Look at the title and the cover. Whose life is the book about? What do you think the turning point will be?
reading.talk: What was the turning point in the story? Have you had a moment like that in your own life? Write three or four sentences, or tell Wehel about it.

quiz.q: I ___ live in a flat above a shop, but now I have a house.
quiz.why: live is a state, not an action, so we use used to.

quiz.q: My parents worked abroad, so my grandparents ___ me up.
quiz.why: bring someone up = look after a child until they are an adult.

quiz.q: The moment when your life starts to go in a new direction is a ___ .
quiz.why: A turning point changes the direction of your life.

quiz.q: The factory ___ in 2009, and four hundred people lost their jobs.
quiz.why: close down = stop doing business for ever.

quiz.q: ___, nobody had a mobile phone. Nowadays everybody has one.
quiz.why: In those days = in the past, at the time you are talking about.

quiz.q: A period of ten years is a ___ .
My father stopped working at sixty-five. He ___ .
quiz.why: retire = stop working, usually because you are older.

quiz.q: You ___ smoke inside the building. It's against the rules.
According to the timetable, the bus ___ at 6.15 every morning.
quiz.why: A timetable uses the present simple: the bus leaves at 6.15.
Have you ever…? asks about your life up to now.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Kwame and Priya's conversation in pairs. Then learners ask each other: Where did you grow up? What did you use to do at the weekend? Listen for a short, smooth used to.
Day 2: then and now. Show an old photo of a town or a street; learners say what people used to do or would do there, and what they do nowadays. Check grow up, bring up and settle down.
Day 3: the task. You are Lena from the history project. Each learner tells their life story in two minutes; the others listen for the turning point and ask one question.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and let two learners read their then-and-now writing aloud.
